## R and RStudio

R is a free professional statistical software that is available for use on Windows, Mac and Linux computers. R is a popular tool for researchers from many fields so acquiring basic R skills will be beneficial for future courses and career plans! 

RStudio is a free software that provides a nice, user friendly interface with R. 


### R Studio server

The quickest way to get started is to go to https://maize.mathcs.carleton.edu, which opens an R Studio window in your web browser. Once logged in, I recommend that you do the following:


  **Step 1:** Create a folder for this course where you can save all of your work. In the **Files**  window, click on New Folder.
  
  ![](step1.png)
  
  **Step 2:** Click on Tools -> Global Options -> R Markdown. Then uncheck the box that says "Show output inline..."
  
  ![](step2.png)
  ![](step3.png)

(It is also possible to download RStudio on your own laptop. Instructions may be found at the end of this document.)


### R Markdown Basics

An R Markdown file (.Rmd file) combines R commands and written analyses, which are 'knit' together into an HTML, PDF, or Microsoft Word document. 

An R Markdown file contains three essential elements:

  **Header:** The header (top) of the file contains information like the document title, author, date and your preferred output format (pdf_document, word_document, or html_document).
  
  **Written analysis:** You write up your analysis after the header and embed R code where needed. The online help below shows ways to add formatting details like bold words, lists, section labels, etc to your final pdf/word/html document. For example, adding ** before and after a word will bold that word in your compiled document.
  
  **R chunks:** R chunks contain the R commands that you want evaluated. You embed these chunks within your written analysis and they are evaluated when you compile the document.

R Markdown example:

  - [Simple R Markdown example](https://clairekelling.com/files/simple_markdown_example.Rmd) 
  
  - [compiled pdf](https://clairekelling.com/files/simple_markdown_example.pdf)

  The following handouts, written by Prof Katie St Clair, contain useful information for making the figured and tables in your compiled documents look nice:
  
  - Graph Formatting: [Markdown.Rmd](https://clairekelling.com/files/graphs_markdown.Rmd) and [pdf](https://clairekelling.com/files/graphs_markdown.pdf)
    
  - Table Formatting: [Markdown.Rmd](https://clairekelling.com/files/tables_markdown.Rmd) file and [pdf](https://clairekelling.com/files/tables_markdown.pdf)
  
  - Graph Formatting: [I'm an inline-style link](https://www.google.com)


## Installing R on your personal computer
Depending on the course, you may be able to complete this course using only the RStudio server described above. However, if you need/want to install RStudio on your personal computer (to be able to use offline, or for work outside of this course), follow these instructions:

1. **Install R:**

      Windows: https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/base/

      Mac: http://cran.r-project.org/bin/macosx/

      Follow the appropriate link above. Complete the default installation.

2. **Install RStudio:**

      Windows or Mac: http://www.rstudio.com/ide/download/

      Follow the link above and select the Desktop version. 

3. **Install LaTeX** (for knitting R Markdown documents to PDF)

      If you want to compile R Markdown to .pdf files, you also need a LaTeX distribution (Note: this is not necessary if you choose to compile as a Word document.)

      Windows: http://www.miktex.org/ (MiKTeX)

      Mac: https://tug.org/mactex/ (MacTeX)

      Follow the appropriate link above. Complete the default installation.
